Lecture 8.5 · Part 1The Eye — Orbit & Eyelids

Lecturer: Dr Shaoyu Wang, Senior Lecturer in Anatomy and Physiology, School of Dentistry and Medical Sciences.

Functions of the eye
Detection of lightConversion of light to action potentials Perception of depthFocusTear production Emotion expression

Location & components

Location — contained in the orbit

  • Inferior to the anterior cranial fossa
  • Anterior to the middle cranial fossa
  • Superolateral to the nasal cavity
  • Superior to the maxillary sinus

Components

  • Eyelids and eyebrows
  • Eyeball
  • Optic nerve
  • Extra-ocular muscles
  • Lacrimal apparatus
  • Adipose tissue, fascia, other nerves and vessels
Dental relevance: the orbit sits directly on the roof of the maxillary sinus, which is why maxillary sinus disease — and surgery near it — can affect the orbit.

Eyelids

The palpebral fissure is the opening between the eyelids.

Layers, superficial → deep
SkinSubcutaneous tissueOrbicularis oculi Tarsus (tarsal plate)Orbital septumConjunctiva

Levator palpebrae superioris opens the upper eyelid; the tarsal (Müller’s) muscle, which is smooth muscle, joins it.

StructureDetail
Orbicularis oculiOrbital part and palpebral part — closes the eyelids; a small lacrimal part helps drain tears
TarsusThick, elongated plates of dense connective tissue — superior and inferior tarsi; contain the tarsal (Meibomian) glands, which secrete a lipid (meibum)
Orbital septaAn extension of periosteum into the eyelids (medial and lateral)

Conjunctiva & lacrimal apparatus

  • Conjunctiva — a transparent mucous membrane; the palpebral part covers the inner surface of the eyelids and the bulbar part covers part of the anterior eyeball
  • Lacrimal gland — at the superolateral corner; produces tears, which reach the eye through its excretory ducts
  • Lacrimal canaliculi and sac — inferomedial, draining tears away
Follow the tear: it is produced superolaterally, swept medially across the eye by blinking, and drains inferomedially — which is why tears run down the inner corner of the eye.

Innervation of the eyelids

Sensory

  • Supraorbital, supratrochlear and lacrimal nerves — V1
  • Infraorbital nerve — V2

Motor

  • Orbicularis oculi — CN VII
  • Levator palpebrae superioris — CN III
  • Superior tarsal muscle — sympathetic fibres
Why ptosis has two flavours: a complete CN III palsy paralyses levator palpebrae superioris and causes a severe droop; loss of sympathetic supply to the superior tarsal muscle (as in Horner's syndrome) causes only a partial droop.

The bony orbit

WallFormed by
RoofOrbital part of the frontal bone
Medial wallPart of the maxilla, the lacrimal bone, the orbital plate of the ethmoid and the palatine bone
FloorMaxilla medially and zygomatic laterally
Lateral wallZygomatic and the greater wing of the sphenoid
ApexLesser wing of the sphenoid, with the optic canal

The inferior orbital fissure transmits the infraorbital nerve and vessels, the zygomatic nerve, and ascending branches from the pterygopalatine ganglion.

Blowout fracture: the orbital floor and medial wall are the thinnest walls, so a blow to the globe tends to fracture the floor downwards into the maxillary sinus — trapping the inferior rectus and causing double vision on upward gaze, plus numbness in the infraorbital nerve territory.

Lecture 8.5 · Part 2Extra-ocular Muscles

  • Levator palpebrae superioris — elevates the upper eyelid
  • Four recti — medial, lateral, superior and inferior
  • Two obliques — superior and inferior
MuscleActionsNerve
Medial rectusAdductionOculomotor (III)
Lateral rectusAbductionAbducent (VI)
Superior rectusElevation, adduction, medial rotationOculomotor (III)
Inferior rectusDepression, adduction, lateral rotationOculomotor (III)
Superior obliqueDepression, abduction, medial rotationTrochlear (IV)
Inferior obliqueElevation, abduction, lateral rotationOculomotor (III)
Levator palpebrae superiorisElevates the upper eyelidOculomotor (III)
The rule to memorise: LR6 SO4 — Lateral Rectus is CN VI, Superior Oblique is CN IV, and everything else (including LPS) is CN III.
Counter-intuitive but worth remembering: the superior oblique depresses the eye and the inferior oblique elevates it — the opposite of what their names suggest. This is because the obliques approach the globe from in front, pulling from a different angle to the recti.

Lecture 8.5 · Part 3The Eyeball

Three tunics
FibrousVascularNervous

Fibrous tunic

PartDetail
ScleraThe white of the eye — dense collagenous connective tissue that the muscles attach to; firm; the posterior ⅚ of the eye
CorneaClear, avascular connective tissue; allows light to enter and refracts light rays; injury prone

Vascular tunic

PartDetail
ChoroidUnderneath the sclera; a thin, black membrane
Ciliary bodyA smooth muscle sphincter plus ciliary processes; attaches to the lens via the suspensory ligaments (zonule fibres)
IrisThe coloured part; smooth muscle that regulates pupil size

The neural tunic is the retina, with an optical (visual) part and a non-visual part.

Chambers of the eyeball

ChamberBetweenContains
Anterior chamberCornea and irisAqueous humor
Posterior chamberIris and lensAqueous humor
Vitreous (postremal) chamberLens and retinaVitreous humor

The anterior and posterior chambers communicate with each other via the pupil.

Innervation & pupil control

Two muscles, two systems: the sphincter pupillae constricts the pupil under parasympathetic control (CN III), while the dilator pupillae widens it under sympathetic control.
Link back to the blood supply lecture: the ophthalmic veins connect the face to the cavernous sinus — the anatomical basis of the “danger triangle”.

Lecture 8.5 · Part 4The Ear — External & Middle

PartContains
External earAuricle, external acoustic meatus (ear canal), tympanic membrane
Middle earTympanic cavity in the petrous temporal bone, and the three auditory ossicles; separated from the external ear by the tympanic membrane
Internal earFluid-filled structures in the petrous temporal bone — a vestibular portion for balance and an auditory portion (cochlea) for hearing

External ear

  • Auricle — elastic cartilage covered by skin
  • Lobule — skin only, no cartilage
  • The tragus and intertragic notch are landmarks for the inferior alveolar nerve block
Directly dental: the tragus and intertragic notch are used to judge the height and angle of the needle when giving an IANB — one of the few places an ear landmark guides a dental injection.
  • About 1 inch long
  • The lateral ⅓ is cartilage; the medial ⅔ is a bony tunnel
  • Covered with skin and hair follicles
  • Modified sweat glands produce cerumen (earwax) — providing lubrication, a protective function, and it is hydrophobic

Tympanic membrane

  • A connective tissue core, lined externally by skin with hair follicles and modified sweat glands, and internally by mucous membrane
  • Its lateral surface faces inferiorly and anteriorly
  • Pars flaccida — the loose portion
  • Pars tensa — the tense portion

Middle ear

Two parts: the tympanic cavity and the epitympanic recess — a cavity in the petrous part of the temporal bone.

WallFormed by / contains
RoofTegmen tympani — a thin plate of bone separating the tympanic cavity from the middle cranial fossa
Lateral wallTympanic membrane
Medial wallPromontory, oval window, round window, pharyngotympanic tube
FloorFundus tympani — a thin plate of bone forming the roof of the jugular foramen

Function: to transmit and amplify vibrations of the tympanic membrane to the internal ear.

Why middle ear infection is taken seriously: only the thin tegmen tympani separates the tympanic cavity from the middle cranial fossa, so infection can spread intracranially.

Ossicles

OssicleParts
MalleusThe largest ossicle — head, neck, anterior process, lateral process, handle
IncusBody, long limb, short limb
StapesHead, anterior limb, posterior limb, base — the base fits into the oval window

Muscles of the middle ear

MuscleAttaches toActionNerve
Tensor tympaniThe handle of the malleusPulls the handle medially to tense the tympanic membrane, reducing the force of vibrations from loud noisesV3
StapediusThe neck of the stapesPulls the stapes posteriorly to stiffen the sound conduction apparatus, preventing excessive oscillationCN VII
Ties back to Bell’s palsy: because stapedius is supplied by the facial nerve, a CN VII lesion can cause hyperacusis — ordinary sounds seeming uncomfortably loud.

Lecture 8.5 · Part 5The Internal Ear

Bony (osseous) labyrinth

  • Located in the petrous portion of the temporal bone
  • Surrounds the membranous labyrinth and contains perilymph, which bathes it
PartDetail
CochleaWith the cochlear canaliculus — the bony canal for the cochlear aqueduct, communicating with the subarachnoid space
VestibuleBetween the cochlea and the semicircular canals; the oval window is on its lateral wall
Semicircular canals (×3)Each with a dilated end, the ampulla, plus the crus commune
Terminology note: a couple of these slides write “semilunar canals”. The accepted term is semicircular canals — “semilunar” belongs to the heart valves.

Membranous labyrinth

Membranous ducts and sacs within the bony labyrinth, containing endolymph.

PartLocationRole
Cochlear duct (scala media)Within the cochleaContains the organ of hearing; the receptor is the spiral organ
SacculeThe smaller, round sacBalance — the cochlear duct drains into it
UtricleThe larger, oval sacBalance — all the semicircular ducts drain into it
Semicircular ducts (×3)Within the semicircular canalsBalance; each has a dilated end, the ampulla

The utriculosaccular duct connects the utricle and saccule to the endolymphatic duct and sac, which attaches to the dura mater.

Keep the two fluids straight: perilymph lies between the bony and membranous labyrinths; endolymph is inside the membranous labyrinth.

Organ of Corti

  • The sensory receptor for hearing
  • Located on the basilar membrane
  • The basilar membrane separates the scala media (cochlear duct) from the scala tympani (tympanic duct)
